parts: In December nineteen forty eight, a man was found dead on a beach in Australia.
He was well dressed. He had no identification at all.
In his pocket was a tiny piece of paper, torn from a book.
It said just two words: "Tamam Shud". Persian for "finished".
More than seventy years later, his identity is still not officially confirmed.
And a five-line code found with him has never been solved.
We will mark every claim: documented, disputed, or still unresolved.
By the end, you will see how one scrap of paper led detectives across the world.
You will hear about a code that top codebreakers still cannot crack.
And you will meet a twist: the scientist leading the case today is married to someone who once thought she was part of this story.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
First, what almost every source agrees on.
On December first, nineteen forty eight, a man's body was found on Somerton Beach, near Adelaide.
No wallet. No labels on most of his clothes. No match to any missing person report.
Doctors who examined him disagreed on the cause of death.
One doctor said it could not have been natural, and suspected a poison.
Another doctor said natural causes were more likely than poisoning.
Even a review in nineteen seventy eight could not name a specific poison.
The body, the date, and that medical disagreement: documented.
A few months later, in January nineteen forty nine, an unclaimed suitcase turned up at Adelaide's train station.
Inside were ordinary clothes, and three items with a sewn-in name tag.
The tag read something close to "Keane", spelled slightly differently each time.
Police searched for a missing "T. Keane" across English-speaking countries.
They never found anyone who matched.
To this day, no one knows who "Keane" really was. Unresolved.
In the dead man's pocket was a hidden scrap of paper.
It had been torn from the last page of a book: a nineteen forty one edition of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam.
Weeks later, a local resident handed in that exact copy of the book.
Inside the back cover, faint pencil marks: a phone number, and five lines of capital letters.
Military code breakers studied those five lines in nineteen seventy eight.
Their conclusion: too few symbols to say anything for certain.
A later team, led by a university professor, spent years testing ciphers on those letters.
Their best guess, decades later, is that each letter stands for the first letter of a word, not a secret message in code.
That is their best guess, not a solved code. It remains unresolved today.
That phone number led police to a nurse who lived near the beach.
She told police she had once owned a copy of that same book.
She said she did not know the dead man.
Police suspected her, but never had enough to charge her with anything.
She is one more thread in the case that was never fully pulled.
Several independent reports agree on this part. Medium-high confidence.
For decades, no one could agree on what, if anything, poisoned him.
Then, in nineteen ninety four, forty five years after the death, a senior judge reviewed the case.
His conclusion: it was most likely a drug called digitalis.
That is a nineteen ninety four opinion, not a nineteen forty nine finding, and the original doctors never agreed on any poison at all.
Disputed, not documented.
For seventy four years, the man had no name.
Then, in July twenty twenty two, a research team said they had one.
Using DNA from hair on an old plaster cast made of his face, compared to distant living relatives, they proposed a name: Carl Webb.
An electrical engineer, born in nineteen oh five, near Melbourne.
The lead researcher called it ninety nine point nine nine percent certain, by his own count.
That is the research team's conclusion, not a court or coroner's ruling.
Police said at the time they still needed more work before confirming it for the coroner.
As of today, that official confirmation has still not been made public.
Separately, in twenty twenty one, the body itself was dug up, to try to get DNA straight from the remains.
That is a different line of investigation from the hair-based identification the year before.
No source confirms whether that exhumation produced a usable result.
So even the proposed name sits in an unusual place: widely reported, not yet closed by any court.
Unresolved, officially.
Here is a strange twist, inside the story itself.
The scientist who led the identification is married to a woman who, for years, believed she might be part of this case.
Through an old family connection, some thought she could be a descendant tied to the nurse's side of the story.
Her husband ran the DNA tests himself.
The result: no match at all. No family link.
The man proving a stranger's identity also tested, and ruled out, his own wife's.
That is documented honesty, inside a case built on uncertainty.
Let us count what we actually know.
The body, the date, the hidden note, and the unsolved code: documented.
The exact poison, and the meaning of those five lines: disputed.
A confirmed, court-closed identity: no evidence found, not yet.
Even the people working the case are not immune to the mystery pulling them in.
So who was the Somerton Man?
Today, a research team has a name. The coroner does not, officially, not yet.
A code still sits unread, after more than seventy years of trying.
It makes you wonder how many answers only look finished, from the outside.
